s: The only museum of its kind in the country
w: Brno is home to the only museum in the country dedicated entirely to Romani history and culture - collecting, researching and displaying a heritage too often left out of national museums altogether. A quiet but significant corrective, tucked into the city's museum landscape.
_facts: Institution dedicated to the history and culture of the Romani people, situated in Brno
Also operates as a publishing house

s: A Gothic giant with 800 years behind it
w: One of the largest well-preserved Gothic churches in the country, this three-nave hall church has stood on Jakubske namesti since the early 13th century. It took until 1995 for the state to formally protect it as a national monument - a late honor for a building that had outlasted most of its neighbors.
_facts: Late Gothic three-nave hall church on Jakubske namesti, central Brno
One of the largest well-preserved Gothic churches in the Czech Republic; history dates to the early 13th century
Categorized as a national monument in 1995

s: Millions of objects, second only to Prague
w: Only Prague's national collection outranks this one: the Moravian Museum is the country's second-largest and second-oldest, holding several million objects spanning science and culture. It's the kind of place that swallows an afternoon without you noticing, exhibits shifting from natural history to fine art and back.
_facts: Second-largest and second-oldest museum in the Czech Republic
Collections include several million objects spanning many fields of science and culture

s: The theatre that switched the lights on first
w: Opened in 1882 as Brno's German-language Stadttheater, this ornate mash-up of Neo-Renaissance, Neo-Baroque and Neoclassical styles claims a genuine world first: one of the earliest public buildings anywhere lit entirely by electric light. Audiences came as much for the novelty overhead as for the play.
_facts: Built as the German Deutsches Stadttheater in 1882
One of the first public buildings in the world lit entirely by electric light
Combines Neo-Renaissance, Neo-Baroque and Neoclassical architectural styles

n: Basilica of the Assumption of Our Lady
s: A queen's rebuild, still stylistically untouched
w: Founded around the year 1000 on the site of an older sanctuary, this convent basilica got its current form fast - built in just eleven years, 1323 to 1334, on orders of Queen Elizabeth Richeza. That speed may explain why it survives as the most stylistically unified Gothic temple in the old Bohemian Crown lands.
_facts: High Gothic convent temple in Old Brno Abbey, founded 980-1020 on the site of a late-10th-century sanctuary
Built 1323-1334 at the instigation of Queen Elizabeth Richeza
Considered the best-preserved stylistically coherent and unified temple in the Lands of the Bohemian Crown

s: Central Europe's oldest theatre, and Mozart played it
w: First mentioned in 1608 and still in use, this is the oldest theatre building in Central Europe - older than the square it stands on suggests. It began as a Renaissance tavern theatre, and in 1767 a teenage Mozart performed here with his sister. It's now folded into the National Theatre Brno's repertoire.
_facts: Built on Zelny trh, Brno's oldest square; began as the Taverna (Tavern) Theatre in Renaissance times
In 1767, Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart performed with his sister here
Building first mentioned in 1608; oldest theatre building in Central Europe; now part of the National Theatre Brno

s: One museum, spread across five palaces
w: The country's second-largest art museum doesn't live in one building - it's spread across five, including the Prazak and Governor's Palaces and a house designed by Jurkovic. Formed in 1961 from a merger of older institutions, it has run the International Biennial of Graphic Design Brno since 1963.
_facts: Second-largest art museum in the Czech Republic, established 1961 by merging two older institutions
Housed across five buildings: Prazak Palace, Governor's Palace, Museum of Applied Arts, Jurkovic House, Josef Hoffmann Museum
Has organized the International Biennial of Graphic Design Brno since 1963

s: The cabbage market that's run since forever
w: Locals still call it the Cabbage Market, and produce stalls still fill this small square in the historic centre much as they always have. At just 0.6 hectares it's easy to cross without noticing, but it's been Brno's working marketplace long enough that the nickname has outlived the official name.
_facts: Square and traditional marketplace in the historic centre of Brno, about 0.6 hectares
German name Kraut Markt, English 'Vegetable Market' or 'Cabbage Market'

s: A hill holding Ice Age fossils in its rock
w: This unassuming hill on Brno's edge is protected as a national nature monument for what's inside it: one of Central Europe's most important paleontological sites, preserving evidence from the Cromerian interglacial deep in the Ice Age. No grand visitor centre, just a quietly significant piece of prehistory.
_facts: Hill and national nature monument in Brno
Mid-Pleistocene, Cromerian interglacial paleontological site, considered the most important of its kind in Central Europe

s: An opera house built facing its composer's house
w: Decades of delay preceded this opera house's 1960 groundbreaking, and when it opened in 1965 its architects made a deliberate choice: the facade faces north, toward the house where composer Leos Janacek once lived. The largest of Brno's three National Theatre stages, it's staged some twenty operas and ballets since.
_facts: Opera house, largest of the three theatres of the National Theatre Brno (with Mahen and Reduta)
Construction began 1960 after decades of delay; opened October 1965; major renovation completed 2018
Facade faces north, away from the city centre, toward the house of its namesake composer Leos Janacek

s: The brick church that stands out by color alone
w: Named simply for its brick-red facade, this Protestant church was designed by Heinrich von Ferstel and built 1863-1867 - a splash of color against Brno's stone-toned skyline. Still active under the Evangelical Church of Czech Brethren, it's protected as a cultural monument as much for its silhouette as its history.
_facts: Protestant church designed by architect Heinrich von Ferstel, built 1863-1867
Used today by the Evangelical Church of Czech Brethren; protected as a cultural monument

s: A margrave's tomb, and Adolf Loos's baptism
w: Founded in the 1350s by Margrave John Henry of Luxembourg, brother of Emperor Charles IV, this church still holds John Henry's tomb before the main altar, alongside his son Jobst. Swedish siege damage in the Thirty Years War left it its current Baroque face. Centuries later, architect Adolf Loos was baptized here.
_facts: Founded mid-14th century by John Henry of Luxembourg, Margrave of Moravia, brother of Charles IV; consecrated 1356
John Henry and his son Jobst of Moravia are buried in a tomb before the main altar; famous polychromed Gothic Pieta of St Thomas inside
Current Baroque appearance dates to rebuilding after Thirty Years War siege damage; architect Adolf Loos was baptized here in 1871

s: The record-crowd stadium reclaimed by trees
w: Once the biggest stadium in Czechoslovakia and still holder of the Czech league's attendance record, this ground was abandoned in 2001 and left to rot - trees through the stands, homeless residents moving in. A former club captain crowdfunded its revival for one last farewell match, drawing 35,000 people back in 2015.
_facts: Closed football stadium, home of FC Zbrojovka Brno, built 1949-1953, biggest stadium in Czechoslovakia through the 1960s-70s
Holds the Czech First League attendance record (Brno vs Slavia Prague, 1996-97 season); closed 2001, fell into disrepair
Captain Petr Svancara led a crowdfunded volunteer restoration for a farewell game; about 35,000 spectators attended on 27 June 2015

w: Nobody knew this was here until 2001, when work under the historic centre rediscovered a 17th-century ossuary holding the remains of an estimated 50,000 people - second in scale in Europe only to the Catacombs of Paris. Part of it sits directly beneath the Church of St James above. Open to visitors since 2012.
_facts: Underground ossuary rediscovered in 2001, partially beneath the Church of St James, Brno
Estimated to hold remains of over 50,000 people; second-largest ossuary in Europe after the Catacombs of Paris
Founded 17th century, expanded 18th century; open to the public since June 2012

w: Laid out originally as the Augarten, this 22.3-hectare green space is both Brno's largest park and the oldest municipal park in the country. Generations of residents have used it exactly as intended - shade, benches and open lawns in the middle of a growing city, civic breathing room that's never gone out of use.
_facts: Originally called Augarten; largest city park in Brno and oldest municipal park in the Czech Republic
Located in the Brno-stred District, covers 22.3 hectares

s: A cave that hid an army command post
w: Ice Age skeletons first drew scientists to this Moravian Karst cave; the 20th century found other uses for it - a phosphate mine, a wartime aircraft factory, later a secret army command post buried in its passages. Only since 2008 has it been open to the public, tours winding through chambers holding a steady chill.
_facts: Show cave in the Moravian Karst Protected Landscape Area, municipality of Krtiny; significant paleontological site with early Quaternary/Pleistocene fauna skeletons
20th-century uses: phosphate clay exploitation, army depot, German factory manufacturing airplane engines, secret command post of the Czechoslovak People's Army
Open for tourist visits since 2008; public tours 600m long, 75 minutes, air temperature 7-8C, humidity around 95%
